items.new: It is the warmest climates that nurse the cruelest fangs: the tiger of Bengal crouches in spiced groves of never-fading green. It is the most dazzling skies that carry the deadliest thunders in their basket: gorgeous Cuba knows tornadoes that never swept tame northern lands. So, too, it is that in these resplendent Japanese seas the mariner meets the most terrible of all storms, the Typhoon. It will sometimes burst out of that cloudless sky like a bomb exploding on a dazed and sleepy town.

items.new: Now, just as the lightning rod on a spire ashore is meant to carry the dangerous fluid off into the soil, so the similar rod that some ships at sea carry to each mast is meant to conduct it into the water. But this conductor must reach down to a considerable depth, so that its end may avoid all contact with the hull; and, moreover, if it were kept towing there all the time, it would be liable to many mishaps, besides interfering more than a little with some of the rigging and more or less slowing the vessel's way through the water. Because of all this, the lower parts of a ship's lightning-rods are not always overboard; they are generally made in long slender links, so that they can more readily be hauled up into the chains (the ledges outside the hull where the shrouds are fastened), or thrown down into the sea, as occasion requires.

items.new: Here it must be said that accidents like this have occurred in more than one case to ships in violent storms. The magnetic energy, as developed in the mariner's needle, is, as everyone knows, essentially one with the electricity seen in the heavens; so it is not much to be wondered at that such things should happen. In instances where the lightning has actually struck the vessel, so as to knock down some of the spars and rigging, the effect on the needle has at times been still more fatal: all its loadstone power has been destroyed, so that the formerly magnetic steel was of no more use than an old wife's knitting needle. But in either case, the needle never again recovers by itself the original power thus marred or lost; and if the binnacle compasses are affected, the same fate reaches all the others that may be in the ship, even if the lowest one were set into the kelson, the timber running along the keel inside the hold.

Then, after repeatedly striking the upper end of this iron rod with the maul, he placed the blunted needle endwise on top of it and hammered that, less strongly, several times, the mate still holding the rod as before. Then, going through some small strange motions with it — whether necessary to the magnetizing of the steel, or merely meant to increase the awe of the crew, is uncertain — he called for linen thread; and moving to the binnacle, he slipped out the two reversed needles there and hung the sail-needle horizontally by its middle over one of the compass-cards. At first the steel went round and round, quivering and vibrating at either end; but at last it settled into its place, and Ahab, who had been intently watching for this result, stepped openly back from the binnacle and, pointing his outstretched arm toward it, exclaimed: "Look for yourselves, and see if Ahab is not lord of the level loadstone! items.new: Though the fated Pequod had now been afloat so long on this voyage, the log and line — a wooden float paid out astern from a reel on a line, to measure the ship's speed — had very seldom been used. Owing to a confident reliance on other means of determining the vessel's position, some merchantmen, and many whalemen, especially when cruising, wholly neglect to heave the log; though at the same time, and often more for form's sake than anything else, they regularly put down on the customary slate the course steered by the ship, as well as the presumed average rate of progress every hour. It had been so with the Pequod. The wooden reel and the angular log attached to it hung, long untouched, just beneath the railing of the after bulwarks. Rain and spray had dampened it; sun and wind had warped it; all the elements had combined to rot a thing that hung so idly. But, heedless of all this, his mood seized Ahab as he happened to glance at the reel, not many hours after the magnet scene; and he remembered that his quadrant was no more, and recalled his frantic oath about the level log and line. The ship was sailing with a plunging motion; astern, the billows rolled in riots.

items.new: At last, when the ship drew near to the outskirts, as it were, of the Equatorial fishing-ground, and in the deep darkness that goes before the dawn was sailing by a cluster of rocky islets, the watch — then headed by Flask — was startled by a cry so plaintively wild and unearthly — like half-articulated wailings of the ghosts of all Herod's murdered Innocents — that one and all, they started from their reveries, and for the space of some moments stood, or sat, or leaned all transfixedly listening, like the carved Roman slave, while that wild cry remained within hearing. The Christian or civilized part of the crew said it was mermaids, and shuddered; but the pagan harpooners remained unappalled. Yet the gray Manxman — the oldest mariner of all — declared that the wild thrilling sounds that were heard were the voices of newly drowned men in the sea.

items.new: "He goes off in a huff. The whole he can endure; at the parts he balks. Now I don't like this. I make a leg for Captain Ahab, and he wears it like a gentleman; but I make a bandbox for Queequeg, and he won't put his head into it. Are all my pains to go for nothing with that coffin? And now I'm ordered to make a life-buoy of it. It's like turning an old coat; going to bring the flesh on the other side now. I don't like this cobbling sort of business — I don't like it at all; it's undignified; it's not my place. Let tinkers' brats do tinkerings; we are their betters. I like to take in hand none but clean, virgin, fair-and-square mathematical jobs, something that regularly begins at the beginning, and is at the middle when midway, and comes to an end at the conclusion; not a cobbler's job, that's at an end in the middle, and at the beginning at the end. It's the old woman's tricks to be giving cobbling jobs. Lord! what an affection all old women have for tinkers. I know an old woman of sixty-five who ran away with a bald-headed young tinker once. And that's the reason I never would work for lonely widow old women ashore, when I kept my job-shop in the Vineyard; they might have taken it into their lonely old heads to run off with me. But heigh-ho! there are no caps at sea but snow-caps. Let me see. Nail down the lid; caulk the seams; pay over the same with pitch; batten them down tight, and hang it with the snap-spring over the ship's stern. Were ever such things done before with a coffin? Some superstitious old carpenters, now, would be tied up in the rigging before they would do the job. But I'm made of knotty Aroostook hemlock; I don't budge. Cruppered with a coffin! Sailing about with a grave-yard tray! But never mind. We workers in woods make bridal-bedsteads and card-tables, as well as coffins and hearses. We work by the month, or by the job, or by the profit; not for us to ask the why and wherefore of our work, unless it be too confounded cobbling, and then we stash it if we can. Hem! I'll do the job, now, tenderly. I'll have me — let's see — how many in the ship's company, all told? But I've forgotten. Anyway, I'll have me thirty separate, Turk's-headed life-lines, each three feet long, hanging all round to the coffin. Then, if the hull goes down, there'll be thirty lively fellows all fighting for one coffin, a sight not seen very often beneath the sun! Come hammer, caulking-iron, pitch-pot, and marling-spike! Let's get to it."
